Read the tide table before the weather. The tide decides where you can
land and when a passage opens; the weather only decides whether you
should go at all.

Wind against tide stacks a steep, short chop that no forecast calls
rough, and it builds fastest on the headlands where the current is
strongest. Around here fog arrives on the afternoon flood and takes the
headlands first, so a bearing to a point that is still visible is worth
more than a screen.

Carry a chart and a compass even with a GPS: the battery is the first
thing to go. Decide the turn-back point on shore, out loud, and turn at
that one — the point invented on the water is always a little further
than it should be.
